title: Preparation of soft tissue samples for synchrotron radiation microtomography and nanotomography
protocol: If the curing agent of Petropoxy 154 is opaque or contains small particles or is crystallized, heat it using a dry bath at 90 ºC until clear.
Cool heated curing agent for one hour to room temperature.
Decant 10 mL of Petropoxy 154 resin into a disposable cup.
Add 1 mL of curing agent by using a disposable syringe.
Mix resin and curing agent thoroughly (over 5 min) using a mixing rod.
Place the cup in a vacuum desiccator and draw a vacuum to degas the resin.
Close the valve when bubbles form to prevent overflow.
Open the valve once the bubbles subside.
Continue drawing the vacuum for at least 6 hours.
Remove the cup from the desiccator and place it in an airtight container.
Store the container in a cold storage chamber (4 ºC).
Degas the resin for one hour prior to every use.
Soak the tissue in 10 mL of ethanol for one hour at room temperature (20–25°C).
Repeat the ethanol soaking process twice in total.
Soak the tissue in another 10 mL of ethanol overnight.
Transfer the tissue to a new vial containing 10 mL of n-butyl glycidyl ether and incubate it for several hours or overnight at room temperature.
Repeat the n-butyl glycidyl ether soaking process twice in total.
Transfer the tissue to a 5 mL vial containing 2 mL of the degassed resin and incubate it overnight at 4°C.
Repeat the resin soaking process twice in total.
If the tissue floats to the surface of the resin, perform an additional soak using another 2 mL of resin.
Cut the sample under a stereomicroscope into small pieces with widths appropriate for analysis (typically 0.5–3.0 mm).
Build an assembly of a borosilicate capillary, transparent plastic tubing with an inner diameter of 3/32", a 3-way stopcock, and a 1 mL syringe.
Turn the stopcock to create an air path through the capillary to the syringe.
Fill the capillary with epoxy resin using a 1-mL syringe.
After the resin reaches the funnel end of the capillary, open the stopcock.
Remove the capillary from the assembly.
Place the tissue sample at the funnel end of the capillary using tweezers or needles.
Gently move the tissue with a tip of tweezers toward the thinner part of the capillary as far as possible.
Insert the capillary into the plastic tubing again while keeping the stopcock open.
Turn the stopcock to re-form the path through the capillary to the syringe.
Push the syringe knob slowly to move the tissue into the capillary.
When the tissue is at the desired position, open the stopcock to settle the tissue.
Cut the capillary with a diamond cutter.
Insert the capillary into a short piece of silicone tubing.
Hold the silicone tubing with tweezers and place the sample in a polypropylene case.
Incubate the case at 90°C for 72–96 hours using a heat dry bath to cure the resin.
Prepare a storage case equipped with a nylon sponge.
Use epoxy glue or double-sided sticky tape to adhere the sponge to the bottom of the case.
Mark sample positions on the sponge and pierce tweezers into the marked positions.
Recover the capillary and pierce it to one of the positions marked on the sponge.
Store the case in a 20°C incubator.
Cut brass tubing to a length of 10–15 mm.
Do not crush the tubing ends when cutting.
Dip the distal end of the capillary in epoxy glue.
Insert the dipped end into the brass tubing.
Wait for the glue to cure.
Store the sample in a sponge case.
Use silicone tubing with an inner diameter of 3–5 mm for casting pellets.
Cut the tubing into a length of 5–10 mm.
Place a droplet of degassed epoxy resin in a polypropylene case.
Stand the tubing on the resin droplet to seal one end.
Cure the resin at 120°C for 15 min using a heat dry bath and then cool it to room temperature.
Fill the tubing with epoxy resin.
Gently insert a resin-soaked sample into the resin-filled tubing.
Incubate the case with the tubing at 90°C for 72–96 hr using a heat dry bath to cure the resin.
Remove the tubing from the case.
Make an incision on the side surface of the silicone tubing.
Peel the tubing from the incision.
Put the sample pellet in a 1.5-mL sampling tube and store it in a 20°C incubator.
Mount capillary samples using an adapter equipped with a set screw.
Ensure the adapter is designed to fit on the nanotomography stage and suit a sleeved sample.
Use a brass adapter for SPring-8 nanotomography beamlines, which has an outer diameter of 10.0 mm.
Screw the invar adapter to a kinematic base for use at the 32-ID beamline of APS.
Mount capillary samples using compound clay for microtomography experiments.
Prepare several adapters having different upper lengths of 20, 25, 30, and 35 mm.
Insert the distal end of the sample into the end hole filled with the clay.
Create a vent hole on the side face of the upper part to prevent sample drifts due to pressurized air remaining in clay.
Attach pellet samples on the flat face of the adapters using epoxy glue or double-sided sticky tape.
For nanotomography experiments, prepare the sample one week in advance to allow for resin curing and mechanical stabilization.
Secure samples with set screws at least one hour prior to data collection to minimize mechanical creep effects.
Place samples in the beamline hutch at least one hour before data collection to equilibrate sample temperature.
Complete sample mounting using clay at least one hour before microtomography data collection to avoid blurring due to mounting.
